report.incidentSummary: At market open (09:15 IST / 03:45 UTC), stock order traffic surged from ~162 req/s to 1,039 req/s on order-service. The upstream broker API immediately throttled order placements with HTTP 429 Too Many Requests due to exceeding a 400 req/s rate limit. This caused broker-connector rate-limit events to spike to 1,047/min and error rates to reach 14.3%. Order-service subsequently exhausted retries, leading to worker thread pool queue saturation, high CPU utilization (86.7%), and an order error rate of ~19.5% between 03:46 and 04:08 UTC before recovering at 04:12 UTC.
report.rootCauseStatement: During the market-open order burst, request volume to broker-api on POST /orders exceeded the provider rate limit of 400 req/s, causing broker-api to return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests. broker-connector passed rate-limit errors to order-service, which exhausted downstream retries and queued worker threads, resulting in ~19.5% of stock orders being rejected between 03:46 and 04:08 UTC.

hypotheses.cause: External broker API enforced a 400 req/s rate limit on POST /orders during market-open traffic burst, returning HTTP 429 Too Many Requests to broker-connector, which exhausted order-service retries and backed up worker thread pools.
hypotheses.rationale: Direct log and metric evidence confirms broker-connector received HTTP 429 responses from broker-api starting at 03:45:00.705 UTC specifically on POST /orders citing a 400 req/s limit. broker-connector rate_limited_count reached 1,047/min and order-service logged 231 instances of orders rejected after retry exhaustion.

hypotheses.cause: order-service replica capacity was insufficient to handle market-open traffic burst, leading to CPU saturation and thread pool queue overflow.
hypotheses.rationale: While order-service experienced elevated CPU (86.7%) and thread pool queue warnings, logs show broker 429 errors began immediately at 03:45:00.705 UTC whereas thread pool queue high-watermark warnings only began at 03:46:37 UTC as a downstream effect of retrying rate-limited requests.

facts.statement: order-service request rate surged at market open from 161.7 req/s at 03:44 UTC to 1,039 req/s at 03:45 UTC, staying above 800 req/s through 03:49 UTC.
order-service error rate rose from ~0.4% up to 19.66% between 03:46 and 04:08 UTC, recovering to ~0.5% by 04:12 UTC.
broker-connector logged 281 HTTP 429 Too Many Requests errors from broker-api on POST /orders (specifying limit 400 req/s; retry-after 1s) between 03:45:00.705 UTC and 04:11:57.035 UTC.
broker-connector rate_limited_count spiked from 0/min to 1,049/min at 03:46 UTC, isolated to endpoint orders (peak 1,047/min).
broker-connector error rate jumped from ~0.2% to 14.34% at 03:46 UTC and remained elevated until 04:11 UTC.
broker-connector p95 upstream latency on orders rose from ~140 ms to a peak of 222.3 ms at 03:47 UTC.

order-service logged 231 instances of 'order rejected: broker rate limit after retries' between 03:45:40 UTC and 04:11:49 UTC, and 18 instances of 'worker thread pool queue length above high watermark' starting at 03:46:37 UTC.
api-gateway error rate on route /v1/orders remained low at ~0.2-0.55% throughout the window.
Database metrics (db_lock_wait_ms, slow_queries_per_min, active_connections, cpu_utilization) and order-service db_pool_wait_ms remained completely healthy and normal.
No deployments or configuration changes were executed on order-service, broker-connector, or database leading up to or during market open.

inferences.statement: The ~19.5% order placement failure rate was directly caused by external broker-api rate limit enforcement on POST /orders rather than internal infrastructure or software regressions.
order-service high CPU (86.7%) and thread pool queue overflow were secondary effects triggered by synchronous retries on rate-limited broker calls under high concurrent volume.
api-gateway error rate remained flat because order-service returned application-level 200/400 domain responses rejecting the orders upon retry exhaustion.

assumptions.statement: broker-connector does not maintain an internal shaping or token-bucket queue for outbound broker orders, forwarding calls directly and surfacing 429 responses back to order-service.

timeline.event: NSE/BSE market open; order-service incoming request rate surges from 161.7 req/s to 1,039 req/s.
broker-connector records first HTTP 429 Too Many Requests response from broker-api on POST /orders (limit 400 req/s).
order-service records first 'order rejected: broker rate limit after retries' log.
broker-connector rate_limited_count peaks at 1,047/min for endpoint orders; error rate peaks at 14.34%; order-service CPU reaches 86.68%.
order-service logs first 'worker thread pool queue length above high watermark' as retry backlog accumulates.
order-service error rate reaches peak of 19.66%.
Last rejected order due to broker rate limit logged by order-service.
broker-connector rate_limited_count drops to 0; order-service error rate returns to normal baseline (0.5%).

confidence.rationale: Direct and sampled log events from broker-connector explicitly cite HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a 400 req/s limit, and order-service explicitly logs order rejections due to broker rate limit exhaustion after retries. Timestamps verify broker rate limiting preceded thread pool queue saturation.

gaps.description: Contractual rate limit agreements with broker-api provider were not directly checked via tool calls.
gaps.impact: Low; provider response payloads explicitly reported 'limit 400 req/s; retry-after 1s'.

recommendedActions.action: Implement client-side rate limiting and request smoothing/token bucket on broker-connector for outbound POST /orders to broker-api capped at 400 req/s with exponential backoff jitter.
recommendedActions.rationale: Prevents sending bursts above the upstream broker quota, eliminating HTTP 429 errors and cascading retries.
recommendedActions.verification: Simulate a market-open burst in staging and observe that broker-connector respects the 400 req/s threshold without triggering upstream 429s.

recommendedActions.action: Engage broker-api provider partner team to negotiate an increased order throughput quota during market open (e.g., 1,000 req/s between 09:14 and 09:30 IST).
recommendedActions.rationale: Market open demand surged to ~1,039 req/s; client-side queueing alone may introduce latency if total allowable rate is strictly 400 req/s.
recommendedActions.verification: Review updated contractual agreement and broker quota dashboard.

recommendedActions.action: Review order-service retry policies to introduce circuit breaking or fail-fast logic when broker-connector detects active 429 throttling.
recommendedActions.rationale: Prevents aggressive synchronous retries from exhausting order-service worker thread pools and driving CPU to 86.7%.
recommendedActions.verification: Trigger upstream mock 429s in load test and confirm order-service worker thread pool watermark remains stable.

incident.title: Stock orders failing at market open
incident.summary: Stock orders started failing at the 09:15 IST open; roughly a quarter of orders error out. order-service CPU is around 90%, so it looks like we are overloaded at the open.
symptoms: order placement errors at market open
incident.userImpact: Users cannot place stock orders at the open.

payload.question: Propose candidate causes before any evidence

candidates.cause: order-service replica capacity saturation due to market-open order burst
candidates.whyPlausible: Retail stock order placement spikes dramatically at the 09:15 IST market open. If order-service autoscaling or pod limits are insufficient, high CPU (90%) and thread starvation would lead to timeouts and dropped orders.
candidates.wouldConfirm: order-service CPU at 90%+ across all pods with request rate spiking sharply at 03:45 UTC, thread pool starvation, and 504/timeout responses generated directly by order-service or api-gateway without downstream errors.

findings.summary: Neither order-service database connection pool exhaustion nor primary database lock contention/slow queries occurred at 03:45 UTC. While order-service db_pool_in_use rose from ~13 to 41.87 connections at 03:45 UTC, db_pool_wait_ms peaked at only 4.83 ms, indicating no pool starvation. Database db_lock_wait_ms (3.91 ms), slow_queries_per_min (4/min), active_connections (~177), and CPU utilization (~38%) were completely normal and stable at 03:45 UTC. Database contention and connection starvation are ruled out as causes for order placement failures.

observations.statement: order-service db_pool_in_use rose from a baseline of ~10-13 connections prior to 03:45 UTC to a peak of 41.87 connections at 03:45 UTC, gradually tapering to ~18-20 connections over the next hour.
order-service db_pool_wait_ms remained very low throughout the entire window, rising marginally from ~2.2-2.7 ms baseline to a peak of 4.83 ms at 03:45 UTC (mean 3.01 ms).
order-service did not experience database connection pool exhaustion or connection starvation at 03:45 UTC, as the pool acquisition wait time peaked at only 4.83 ms.
database db_lock_wait_ms was completely flat across the investigation window (min 3.45 ms, max 4.57 ms, mean 3.98 ms), measuring 3.91 ms at 03:45 UTC.
database slow_queries_per_min remained within normal baseline levels (0 to 8 queries/min, mean 2.9/min), with 4 queries/min at 03:45 UTC.
database active_connections (177 at 03:45 UTC, mean 176.1) and cpu_utilization (38.38% at 03:45 UTC, mean 36.93%) showed no anomalies or spikes at market open.
The primary database suffered no lock contention, slow query degradation, or resource saturation at 03:45 UTC. Database bottleneck and pool starvation are eliminated as root causes.

findings.summary: No deployments, configuration changes, or infrastructure changes occurred for order-service, broker-connector, or database leading up to or during market open. Past incident PIR-2008 exhibits identical symptoms (order-service CPU saturation and timeouts at 09:15 IST market open), which was caused by insufficient order-service replica capacity/autoscaling floor at market open.

observations.statement: There were zero deployments, configuration changes, or infrastructure changes to order-service, broker-connector, or database between 2026-10-11T21:15:00.000Z and 2026-10-12T05:15:00.000Z.

The only change across all services during the window was CHG-48484 on mf-order-service (feature flag order_ticket_redesign rollout 25% -> 55% at 2026-10-12T04:31:16.862Z), which occurred well after the 03:45:00Z market open incident start.

Prior changes to the scoped services in the preceding 7 days were CHG-48339 (broker-connector feature flag on 2026-10-06) and CHG-48419 (order-service node pool OS patch on 2026-10-08), neither of which occurred near the incident onset.

Past incident PIR-2008 (SEV2, 2026-08-31T03:45:00.000Z) had identical symptoms: order-service CPU pinned/saturated at 09:15 IST market open with order latency rising to 3s and timeouts. Its root cause was too few order-service replicas for the opening rush, resolved by raising the autoscaling floor before 09:00 IST.

Because no deployments or config changes were introduced leading up to market open, the failure pattern strongly points to an autoscaling/capacity or market-open load rush issue similar to PIR-2008 rather than a software regression.

Around 03:45 UTC (market open at 09:15 IST), broker-connector experienced severe upstream rate limiting from broker-api on POST /orders (HTTP 429 Too Many Requests, limit 400 req/s). This caused rate_limited_count on orders to surge up to 1047/min, error_rate to spike to ~14.3% (from ~0.2%), and p95 upstream latency on orders to increase from ~140ms to 222ms between 03:45 and 04:11 UTC.

observations.statement: broker-connector rate_limited_count spiked from 0/min baseline to 1049/min at 03:46 UTC and remained elevated (ranging between 229.5/min and 1049/min) until 04:11 UTC, returning to 0 at 04:12 UTC. The rate limiting was almost entirely isolated to endpoint 'orders' (peak 1047/min at 03:46 UTC).

broker-connector error_rate jumped from a normal baseline of ~0.2% up to ~14.3% between 03:46 UTC and 04:08 UTC, before tapering down (10.71% at 04:09, 7.17% at 04:10, 3.70% at 04:11) and returning to ~0.2% at 04:12 UTC.

broker-connector upstream_latency_p95_ms increased across endpoints starting at 03:45 UTC: 'orders' latency rose from ~130-150ms to 213.0ms at 03:45 UTC and peaked at 222.3ms at 03:47 UTC; 'quotes' rose from ~120-140ms to 199.8ms at 03:45 UTC and 213.8ms at 03:46 UTC; 'holdings' rose from ~100-110ms to 179.8ms at 03:45 UTC.

# Investigation report: Stock orders failing at market open

**Outcome:** conclusive · **Stop reason:** critic_accepted · **Confidence:** 0.95 · **Written by:** reporting agent

## Summary
At market open (09:15 IST / 03:45 UTC), stock order traffic surged from ~162 req/s to 1,039 req/s on order-service. The upstream broker API immediately throttled order placements with HTTP 429 Too Many Requests due to exceeding a 400 req/s rate limit. This caused broker-connector rate-limit events to spike to 1,047/min and error rates to reach 14.3%. Order-service subsequently exhausted retries, leading to worker thread pool queue saturation, high CPU utilization (86.7%), and an order error rate of ~19.5% between 03:46 and 04:08 UTC before recovering at 04:12 UTC.

**Root cause:** During the market-open order burst, request volume to broker-api on POST /orders exceeded the provider rate limit of 400 req/s, causing broker-api to return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests. broker-connector passed rate-limit errors to order-service, which exhausted downstream retries and queued worker threads, resulting in ~19.5% of stock orders being rejected between 03:46 and 04:08 UTC.

## Hypotheses
1. **External broker API enforced a 400 req/s rate limit on POST /orders during market-open traffic burst, returning HTTP 429 Too Many Requests to broker-connector, which exhausted order-service retries and backed up worker thread pools.** — `broker-connector`, rate_limiting_or_quota, confidence 0.88, supported
   - Supporting: [ev_1, ev_3, ev_9, ev_10, ev_11, ev_13, ev_18, ev_21, ev_22] · Contradicting: none
   - Direct log and metric evidence confirms broker-connector received HTTP 429 responses from broker-api starting at 03:45:00.705 UTC specifically on POST /orders citing a 400 req/s limit. broker-connector rate_limited_count reached 1,047/min and order-service logged 231 instances of orders rejected after retry exhaustion.
2. **order-service replica capacity was insufficient to handle market-open traffic burst, leading to CPU saturation and thread pool queue overflow.** — `order-service`, capacity_saturation, confidence 0.12, ruled_out
   - Supporting: [ev_7, ev_10, ev_17, ev_19, ev_21] · Contradicting: [ev_18, ev_22]
   - While order-service experienced elevated CPU (86.7%) and thread pool queue warnings, logs show broker 429 errors began immediately at 03:45:00.705 UTC whereas thread pool queue high-watermark warnings only began at 03:46:37 UTC as a downstream effect of retrying rate-limited requests.

## Facts
- order-service request rate surged at market open from 161.7 req/s at 03:44 UTC to 1,039 req/s at 03:45 UTC, staying above 800 req/s through 03:49 UTC. [ev_10]
- order-service error rate rose from ~0.4% up to 19.66% between 03:46 and 04:08 UTC, recovering to ~0.5% by 04:12 UTC. [ev_9]
- broker-connector logged 281 HTTP 429 Too Many Requests errors from broker-api on POST /orders (specifying limit 400 req/s; retry-after 1s) between 03:45:00.705 UTC and 04:11:57.035 UTC. [ev_18, ev_22]
- broker-connector rate_limited_count spiked from 0/min to 1,049/min at 03:46 UTC, isolated to endpoint orders (peak 1,047/min). [ev_1, ev_3]
- broker-connector error rate jumped from ~0.2% to 14.34% at 03:46 UTC and remained elevated until 04:11 UTC. [ev_11]
- broker-connector p95 upstream latency on orders rose from ~140 ms to a peak of 222.3 ms at 03:47 UTC. [ev_13]
- order-service logged 231 instances of 'order rejected: broker rate limit after retries' between 03:45:40 UTC and 04:11:49 UTC, and 18 instances of 'worker thread pool queue length above high watermark' starting at 03:46:37 UTC. [ev_21]
- api-gateway error rate on route /v1/orders remained low at ~0.2-0.55% throughout the window. [ev_24]
- Database metrics (db_lock_wait_ms, slow_queries_per_min, active_connections, cpu_utilization) and order-service db_pool_wait_ms remained completely healthy and normal. [ev_4, ev_5, ev_6, ev_8, ev_15, ev_16]
- No deployments or configuration changes were executed on order-service, broker-connector, or database leading up to or during market open. [ev_2, ev_12, ev_14]

## Inferences
- The ~19.5% order placement failure rate was directly caused by external broker-api rate limit enforcement on POST /orders rather than internal infrastructure or software regressions. [ev_1, ev_3, ev_9, ev_11, ev_18, ev_21, ev_22]
- order-service high CPU (86.7%) and thread pool queue overflow were secondary effects triggered by synchronous retries on rate-limited broker calls under high concurrent volume. [ev_7, ev_10, ev_21]
- api-gateway error rate remained flat because order-service returned application-level 200/400 domain responses rejecting the orders upon retry exhaustion. [ev_21, ev_24]

## Assumptions
- broker-connector does not maintain an internal shaping or token-bucket queue for outbound broker orders, forwarding calls directly and surfacing 429 responses back to order-service.

## Timeline
- **2026-10-12 09:15:00 IST (03:45:00 UTC)** NSE/BSE market open; order-service incoming request rate surges from 161.7 req/s to 1,039 req/s. [ev_10]
- **2026-10-12 09:15:00.705 IST (03:45:00.705 UTC)** broker-connector records first HTTP 429 Too Many Requests response from broker-api on POST /orders (limit 400 req/s). [ev_18, ev_22]
- **2026-10-12 09:15:40.112 IST (03:45:40.112 UTC)** order-service records first 'order rejected: broker rate limit after retries' log. [ev_21]
- **2026-10-12 09:16:00 IST (03:46:00 UTC)** broker-connector rate_limited_count peaks at 1,047/min for endpoint orders; error rate peaks at 14.34%; order-service CPU reaches 86.68%. [ev_1, ev_3, ev_7, ev_11]
- **2026-10-12 09:16:37.315 IST (03:46:37.315 UTC)** order-service logs first 'worker thread pool queue length above high watermark' as retry backlog accumulates. [ev_21]
- **2026-10-12 09:22:00 IST (03:52:00 UTC)** order-service error rate reaches peak of 19.66%. [ev_9]
- **2026-10-12 09:41:49 IST (04:11:49 UTC)** Last rejected order due to broker rate limit logged by order-service. [ev_21]
- **2026-10-12 09:42:00 IST (04:12:00 UTC)** broker-connector rate_limited_count drops to 0; order-service error rate returns to normal baseline (0.5%). [ev_1, ev_9, ev_11]

## Confidence
0.95: Direct and sampled log events from broker-connector explicitly cite HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with a 400 req/s limit, and order-service explicitly logs order rejections due to broker rate limit exhaustion after retries. Timestamps verify broker rate limiting preceded thread pool queue saturation.

## Gaps
- Contractual rate limit agreements with broker-api provider were not directly checked via tool calls. (impact: Low; provider response payloads explicitly reported 'limit 400 req/s; retry-after 1s'.)

## Recommended actions (not executed)
- **[now]** Implement client-side rate limiting and request smoothing/token bucket on broker-connector for outbound POST /orders to broker-api capped at 400 req/s with exponential backoff jitter. [ev_18, ev_22]
  - Why: Prevents sending bursts above the upstream broker quota, eliminating HTTP 429 errors and cascading retries.
  - Verify: Simulate a market-open burst in staging and observe that broker-connector respects the 400 req/s threshold without triggering upstream 429s.
- **[next]** Engage broker-api provider partner team to negotiate an increased order throughput quota during market open (e.g., 1,000 req/s between 09:14 and 09:30 IST). [ev_10, ev_18]
  - Why: Market open demand surged to ~1,039 req/s; client-side queueing alone may introduce latency if total allowable rate is strictly 400 req/s.
  - Verify: Review updated contractual agreement and broker quota dashboard.
- **[next]** Review order-service retry policies to introduce circuit breaking or fail-fast logic when broker-connector detects active 429 throttling. [ev_7, ev_21]
  - Why: Prevents aggressive synchronous retries from exhausting order-service worker thread pools and driving CPU to 86.7%.
  - Verify: Trigger upstream mock 429s in load test and confirm order-service worker thread pool watermark remains stable.

Cited evidence: ev_1, ev_2, ev_3, ev_4, ev_5, ev_6, ev_7, ev_8, ev_9, ev_10, ev_11, ev_12, ev_13, ev_14, ev_15, ev_16, ev_17, ev_18, ev_19, ev_21, ev_22, ev_24
